          Arsenal’s WSL Season is in Peril, But Can They Find Answers?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 21, 2026
          
                      Maya Shah / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Arsenal’s season is threatening to unravel, with defensive frailties, a blunt attack and increasingly puzzling selection decisions leaving Renée Slegers under growing pressure. Can the Dutch coach find the answers, or do the problems run deeper than results suggest?

The noise around Renée Slegers is becoming impossible to drown out. Every poor result adds another decibel, and when the boos rang out at the Emirates on Saturday, the discontent was no longer confined to social media; it had reached the stands.

Arsenal’s 1–1 draw with Birmingham City, a side still searching for its first win of their new WSL era, laid bare a team short of attacking conviction and defensive authority, while becoming the second time this season that Slegers side have failed to beat newly promoted opposition at home – their longest such run against those teams in the competition. The Gunners only found any real impetus after falling behind.

The result extended their winless league run to five games, the longest in the club’s history. The irony is stark: barely three matches earlier, Arsenal had been celebrating a record 20-game unbeaten league run. Now, their season is unravelling just as quickly as it once gathered momentum.
Slegers remained composed in her post-match interview, but her words carried a significance that her demeanour concealed.

For the first time, she openly acknowledged that change might be necessary: “Everything I want is the best for us, and all the best for these players,” she said. “I think if that’s not the case anymore, then a change needs to happen. But I have belief in knowing where we can go with this team.”

The question is whether that belief is being matched by evidence on the pitch. Arsenal look increasingly susceptible defensively and toothless against low blocks. Their attacking patterns lack variation, their personnel and positional roles invite questions, and Slegers’ continued reshuffling of the starting XI raises doubts over whether she has identified a system capable of consistently getting the best out of it.

Before the international break, the Arsenal boss insisted that the title race was “not in the conversation.” Now, the more immediate concern seems to be whether Arsenal can salvage their push for Champions League qualification, with a nine-point gap to close on third-place London City Lionesses. Europe is far from a foregone conclusion and complacency is no longer an option.

The question, then, is not simply whether Slegers can turn Arsenal’s season around, but whether the problems run deeper than just results; into the team’s tactical structure, the leadership, and their ability to impose themselves on opponents. Because until Arsenal find answers to those questions, the noise is unlikely to subside.

Arsenal’s defence has been assailable at times, rarely more illustrated than the bizarre decision made by vice-captain Leah Williamson in the Champions League to handle the ball in the penalty area against Paris FC to inadvertently allow a late equaliser.

It was the second time since last season that Arsenal had failed to win a Champions League match after leading by two or more goals. They had never done so in the competition between 2001-02 and 2024-25.
Though interestingly, their defensive problems are not necessarily reflected in the volume of chances they are conceding. Instead, the concern is the quality of those opportunities.

Against Birmingham, Arsenal were exposed by fast breaks for the second consecutive game, with Ona Batlle unable to recover and Lotte Wubben-Moy failing to intercept Neve Herron's ball that split the Gunners' defence in two.

Birmingham attempted three shots from fast breaks against Arsenal; only Aston Villa, with four also against the Gunners in April 2025, have managed more in a WSL match. More concerningly, Birmingham did not win possession in Arsenal’s final third for any of those opportunities, demonstrating how effectively they could threaten from deeper positions.

Indeed, Arsenal have now conceded six shots from fast breaks this season, with only Liverpool conceding more (seven). They have also conceded two goals from such situations, the joint-most in the league alongside Liverpool and London City.
One explanation for that is their carelessness on the ball.

Arsenal are losing possession 147.8 times per game, their highest average since 2023-24 (151.4). Yet, they are facing just seven shots per game, the second-lowest average in a WSL season in their recorded history, behind only 2025-26 (6.9).
That apparent contradiction is revealing. Arsenal are not allowing opponents to shoot frequently, but their defensive lapses are proving costly when they do.

The broader expected-goals (xG) data reinforces the concern. Arsenal are conceding 0.91 expected goals against (xGA) per game, their second-highest figure after the 2024-25 campaign (0.95). Moreover, the Gunners' 0.94 expected goals on target against (xGOT) per game is also among their highest seasonal averages, while their xG per shot faced of 0.13 is a record high for the club.
Williamson’s role in this decline deserves scrutiny, although the data offers a more nuanced picture than a straightforward loss of form.
